title: The Baal Shem Tov
hook: Israel ben Eliezer, an eighteenth-century teacher in Podolia, taught that God is found in joy and simple devotion

segments.voice: Yesterday we closed our taste of Talmud with Daf Yomi. Your line was a page a day. Did you read one short passage? Today, a new part of the path begins. Day two hundred ninety-four.

Picture a village in what's now Ukraine, about three hundred years ago. Most of the Jews there are poor. Farmers, innkeepers, peddlers, wagon drivers. Many can barely read the prayers, let alone a page of Talmud. The great scholars are far away, and sometimes what people hear is that real closeness to God belongs to the learned. Then a man starts walking from village to village with a very different message. His name was Israel ben Eliezer. People came to call him the Baal Shem Tov.
screen: `A VILLAGE, THREE HUNDRED YEARS AGO.` → `POOR, AND BARELY READING.` → `A DIFFERENT MESSAGE.`

segments.voice: Baal Shem Tov means master of the good name. People often shorten it to the Besht. He lived in the 1700s, in the region called Podolia, and settled in the town of Medzhybizh. He wrote almost nothing himself. What we know comes through his students, and through a book of stories about him printed decades after his death, so history and legend are woven together. His message, as his students taught it, was simple and radical. God is everywhere, in every place and every moment, so every moment can be a way to God. Not only study and prayer, but eating, working, walking, talking with a neighbor. And the way in is joy. He's remembered for teaching that sadness shuts the heart, and that a person should serve God joyfully. His followers pointed to a line from the Psalms: "Serve the LORD with gladness." The movement that grew from his teaching is called Hasidism, and its followers Hasidim. Hasid is an old word, from the Hebrew chesed, loving-kindness. In the Psalms a hasid is a devoted, faithful one. Not everyone welcomed the movement at first; some leading rabbis, called Mitnagdim, opposed it strongly. Over time both became part of the wide fabric of Jewish life. For the next weeks, we'll hear Hasidic stories: short, surprising, and full of joy.
screen: `MASTER OF THE GOOD NAME.` · `GOD IN EVERY MOMENT.` · `SERVE WITH GLADNESS.` · `HASID: FROM CHESED, DEVOTION.` · then, large: `SERVE WITH JOY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, and a look back at this week: Kamtza and Bar Kamtza, give me Yavneh, the white face, peace over precision, most from my students, a page a day. Now settle, and breathe. Think of one ordinary task you'll do today. Dishes. The commute. Folding laundry. Answering email. Picture doing it with a little joy on purpose. Humming. Noticing the warm water. Being glad your hands work. Not pretending it's thrilling, just letting gladness in. The bell holds the time.
Hasid. A devoted one, from chesed, loving-kindness. The followers of the Baal Shem Tov, who taught that God is found in joy.
Your line: serve with joy. Today, do one ordinary task gladly, as if it matters. Day two hundred ninety-four.

howItsDone: Hasidic communities today, such as Chabad, Satmar and Breslov, follow teachings that trace back to the Baal Shem Tov, and joyful song and dance, the niggun, are central to their prayer and gatherings.

original.note: Hebrew: a devoted, pious one, from chesed, loving-kindness.

trapdoor: what you thought: men in black hats.
what it means: a devoted one, and a movement built on joy and closeness to God everywhere.
what a scholar hears: the Besht left almost no writings; Shivchei HaBesht, the book of his praises, was printed in 1814–15, decades after his death in 1760.

sources.work: Hasidic teachings attributed to the Baal Shem Tov

notes: Opens 'Hasidic stories' (days 294–313) and includes the week-end look-back for days 288–294.
Dates: the Baal Shem Tov c. 1698/1700–1760; settled in Medzhybizh (Międzybóż) c. 1740. Shivchei HaBesht printed 1814 (Kapust/Berdichev), Yiddish 1815.
The teaching on joy and against sadness is found in Tzava'at HaRivash and his students' works; attribution to the Besht himself is traditional.
Mitnagdim described neutrally; the Vilna Gaon's opposition is not named. Hasidic groups in howItsDone are examples only.
